newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Study shows impact of mining on W.Australia.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Study shows impact of mining on W.Australia.

text.p: A study of the macroeconomic effects of new investment in Western Australia's resource industry has found "substantial and far reaching flow-on benefits", including annual increases in gross state product and consumption of around three percent.

The study of 35 mining and mineral processing projects committed or under construction and worth a total of $A5.3 billion also found the value of Western Australia exports will temporarily fall during construction by about 12 percent a year.

However, it concluded that this effect was more than offset by a five percent higher than otherwise level of Western Australia exports sustained (annually) throughout the much longer production phase of the projects.
The results of the University of Western Australia study were released by Resources Development Minister Colin Barnett.

The study is part of a three-year research programme entitled "Minerals East Asia and the W.A. Economy" being carried out by a team headed by Ken Clements, Dean Economics and Commerce at the university and funded by the Chamber of Mines and Energy.
Clements said the study used a new general equilibrium model of the state economy to simulate the broader economy-wide effects of the investment surge associated with the 35 projects.
One of the key results was an estimate of 39,200 new jobs in a typical year of the construction phase and 22,000 new jobs across the state economy during the production phase.
"Interestingly in the construction phase we have job losses in the mining and mineral processing sector and the agricultural, forestry and fishing sector," Clements said.
"What's going on here is that, during the construction phase that's going to generate some appreciation of the real exchange rate," he said.
"That is, costs will rise relative to the exchange rate, which will serve to squeeze these export industries," he said.
"In the production phase employment in all sectors expands, however. These are permanent jobs and interestingly it is the service sectors that increase the most," he said.
"Again the education, health and welfare sector, and the wholesale trade, retail trade and entertainment sector are the two largest gainers," he said.
"Although mining and mineral processing is the stimulus for that growth, it only adds 3,200 jobs or something less than 20 per cent of the total increase," he said.
